0.title: When You Cannot Go Back
0.essay:
It may come at three in the morning, or in the car, or when an old song plays. A memory rises: a decision made years ago, words you cannot unsay, a road you took or refused. And with it comes the ache of two small words: if only. If only I had stayed. If only I had left. If only I had listened. If you know that ache, this study is for you.

What cannot be undone

Some wrongs can be put right with an apology or a phone call. Others cannot. A marriage that ended. Children now grown, raised in ways you would do differently. Years given to the wrong things. A career chosen in haste, or a calling turned down. An abortion. Harm done to someone who is now out of reach. Time runs only one way, and that is part of what makes regret so heavy. You cannot go back.

The Bible does not look away from this. Its pages are full of people who did what they could not undo: David, Peter, Paul, Jacob and his sons. They lived with consequences that did not go away. Yet in every one of their stories, the past was not the last word. God was.

Where we are going

This study names regret honestly and looks at what lies beneath the endless “what if”. It sets out the two kinds of grief Paul describes, one leading to life and one to death. Then it brings the gospel to the past: a forgiveness that is full, a Saviour who restores those who failed him, and a God who weaves even our worst choices into his good purposes without ever calling them good. It ends with practical wisdom for living with the past.

The studies Forgiveness & Reconciliation and Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation cover God’s pardon, making peace with others and the inner accuser. This study looks at one thing: the past itself, and how to live with it before God.

The chapters

If Only; Two Kinds of Grief; A Past Blotted Out; The Rooster and the Charcoal Fire; God Meant It for Good; and Living with the Past.

For reflection

What memory most often brings the words “if only” to your mind? When it comes, what do you usually do with it?

1.title: If Only
1.essay:
Regret is the pain of looking back and wishing it had been otherwise. Everyone feels it at times. For some it is a passing sting. For others it is a room they live in, replaying the same scene year after year, rewriting the ending, and waking to find it unchanged.

The replay

Regret has a familiar shape. The mind returns to the moment of choice: the day you signed, the night you said it, the year you were too busy. It plays the scene again, slowly. Then it begins to imagine the other life, the one that might have been. What if I had married someone else, or not married at all? What if I had taken that job, or stayed home with the children? What if I had seen the signs in time? Each replay ends the same way, and each one hurts a little more.

Thinking over the past is not wrong. Scripture tells us to remember and learn. But there is a kind of thinking that goes round and round without arriving anywhere. Doctors call it rumination. It feels like working on the problem, but it is closer to pacing a cell. Nothing is learned, nothing is mended, and the heart grows heavier.

Not all regret is the same

It helps to tell apart three kinds of regret, because each needs something different.

Regret over sin. Some of what we regret was wrong: cruel words, unfaithfulness, dishonesty, an abortion, years of neglect, harm done to the weak. This regret is guilt, and guilt needs forgiveness. Only God can give that fully, and he does.

Regret over unwise choices. Some of what we regret was not sin at all. You chose a course, a house, a job or a town, and it turned out badly. You trusted someone who let you down. This regret is about foolishness, or simply about not knowing what you could not have known. It needs wisdom and humility, not repentance. Treating every poor decision as a sin only adds false guilt to real sorrow. The study Knowing God’s Will looks at how we make decisions in freedom.

Regret over what was done to us, or what simply happened. Some people carry “if only” about things they never chose: a parent who left, an illness, a loss. This is grief, not guilt. It needs comfort and lament.

Often the three are tangled together. A broken marriage may hold real sin on both sides, unwise choices made in youth, and wounds that were never your fault. Part of the healing is to let God separate the strands, so that you repent of what was sin, learn from what was folly, and grieve what was loss.

A brother’s blood

Joseph’s brothers sold him into slavery and told their father he was dead. About twenty years later, in trouble in Egypt, they said to one another, “In truth we are guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us and we did not listen” (Genesis 42:21). They had carried that memory the whole time. They still remembered his face and his pleading. Unconfessed regret does not fade with time. It waits.

An old man’s summary

Their father Jacob had his own long list. He had deceived his blind father and cheated his brother out of the blessing. His favouritism had helped turn his sons against one another. When Pharaoh asked his age, Jacob answered, “Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life” (Genesis 47:9). It is the voice of a man looking back and seeing mostly loss. Many older believers know that voice.

Yet Jacob’s story did not end there, as a later chapter will show. And even Esau, who “sold his birthright for a single meal” (Hebrews 12:16), stands as a warning, not of someone who wanted God and was refused, but of someone who wanted back what he had thrown away while still not wanting God. Tears over lost blessings are not the same as turning to the Lord.

Regret is a sign of life

Painful as it is, regret means your conscience is alive. The person who regrets nothing is usually not innocent but hardened. To ache over what you did is to know, at some level, that you were made for something better. That ache can drive you away from God, into hiding and despair. Or it can drive you to him. The rest of this study is about which way it goes.

An example

A man in his sixties retires and finds, for the first time in decades, that he has time to think. What he thinks about is his son, now forty and distant. He remembers the football matches he missed, the sharp words at the dinner table, the way he chose overtime again and again. Every evening on his walk he replays a different scene. He tells no one. His wife only notices that he has grown quiet.

For reflection

When you look back, which of the three kinds of regret do you carry: sin, unwise choices, or things that happened to you? Are any of them tangled together? Do you find yourself replaying the past without arriving anywhere? What would it mean to bring that replay to God rather than keep it to yourself?

2.title: Two Kinds of Grief
2.essay:
Two men betrayed Jesus on the same night. Both were sorry afterwards. Both wept, or wished they could undo what they had done. One went out and took his own life. The other became a pillar of the church. The difference was not the size of their sin. It was the kind of grief that followed it.

Paul’s distinction

Paul had written a painful letter to the church in Corinth, and it hurt them. Later he wrote, “For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). There are two kinds of sorrow over wrongdoing. They can feel alike from the inside, with the same tears and sleeplessness. But they lead in opposite directions.

Notice the phrase “without regret”. Godly grief leads somewhere you will never be sorry to have gone. It ends. It does its work and gives way to life. Worldly grief does not end. It feeds on itself, and its fruit is death: of joy, of hope, sometimes of the body itself.

Judas and Peter

When Judas saw that Jesus was condemned, “he changed his mind” and brought back the silver, saying, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matthew 27:3–4). His words were true. His remorse was real. But it took him only to the priests, who said, “What is that to us? See to it yourself” (Matthew 27:4). With no hope of mercy, he went and hanged himself.

That same night Peter denied Jesus three times. As the rooster crowed, “the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61). Peter remembered what Jesus had said, “and he went out and wept bitterly” (Luke 22:62). His tears were as bitter as any. But they were wept within reach of that look. He stayed with the other disciples, and he was there when the women came with news of the empty tomb.

Judas was sorry for what he had done. Peter was sorry, and still turned toward Jesus. Worldly grief looks at the sin and at oneself. Godly grief looks at the sin and at the Lord.

What lies beneath worldly grief

Worldly grief is often less about God than we think. Beneath it, several things may be at work.

The lost self. Much regret is grief over the person I thought I was. “I am not the kind of person who does that.” But I did. The pain is wounded pride as much as sorrow for the harm done.

The lost life. Some regret mourns the life I had planned: the career, the reputation, the family photograph. When that life was an idol, its loss feels like the loss of everything.

Control. The “if only” quietly assumes that everything hung on me. If I had chosen better, all would have been well. It is a strange kind of pride, as though the whole story depended on my getting it right.

Penance. Many people keep reliving their failures because, deep down, they feel they ought to suffer for them. The replay becomes a payment. If I hurt enough, for long enough, perhaps it will be squared. This feels like humility, but it is an attempt to atone for ourselves, and it never works.

Each of these keeps the eyes on self. That is why worldly grief cannot heal. It has no one outside itself to go to.

The marks of godly grief

Godly grief has a different direction. It begins with God: “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4). It grieves the wrong done, not only the loss suffered. It is honest, without excuses. It moves toward action, Paul says, producing “earnestness” and “eagerness to clear yourselves” (2 Corinthians 7:11). And it trusts that there is mercy. Godly grief can be very deep, but it has hope at the bottom of it.

The test is not how much you feel. Some people weep easily and change little. Others feel numb and yet are truly turning to God. The test is where your grief takes you: into yourself, or to Christ.

Nostalgia’s cousin

There is a gentler form of looking back that also needs care. “Say not, ‘Why were the former days better than these?’ For it is not from wisdom that you ask this” (Ecclesiastes 7:10). Endless longing for the past, whether for what we did or what we had, can become a refusal to live in the present God has given. God’s people are always pilgrims facing forward.

An example

A woman in her forties had an affair that ended her first marriage. She has since married again and come to faith. Yet every anniversary of the divorce she sinks into days of self-reproach. A wise friend asks her what she hopes those days will achieve. After a long silence she says, “I suppose I think I deserve them.” It is the first time she has seen that her sorrow has become a way of paying.

When grief turns dark

Judas’ story is a warning to take seriously. Remorse without hope can become despair, and despair can kill. If your regret has brought you to the point of thinking that others would be better off without you, or that you cannot go on, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust today. Peter’s road is open to you.

For reflection

When you feel sorrow over the past, does it take you into yourself or toward Christ? Which of the four, the lost self, the lost life, control or penance, do you recognise in your own regret? Is there any sense in which you are trying to pay for your past by suffering over it? What would godly grief look like for you now?

3.title: A Past Blotted Out
3.essay:
The gospel does not tell you that your past was better than it was. It tells you something far more surprising: that the worst of it has been dealt with, completely, by someone else. The record is not edited. It is paid.

A king with blood on his hands

David committed adultery with Bathsheba, then arranged for her husband Uriah to be killed in battle to cover it up. For months he said nothing. Then the prophet Nathan told him a story about a rich man who stole a poor man’s only lamb, and when David burned with anger, Nathan said, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). David answered simply, “I have sinned against the LORD.” And Nathan replied, “The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Samuel 12:13).

Few sins could be harder to undo. A man was dead. A family was shattered. And yet the forgiveness came at once. It did not wait for years of penance. It came the moment David stopped hiding.

The prayer of a regretful man

Psalm 51, by its heading, comes from this moment. It is the prayer of a man who knows exactly what he has done. “For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me” (Psalm 51:3). That is regret’s experience: the sin always there, in front of the eyes. But David does not stay staring at it. He turns to God’s character: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions” (Psalm 51:1).

He asks for three things regret cannot give itself. Cleansing: “wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 51:7). A new heart: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10). And restored joy: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Psalm 51:12). David did not expect to feel happy about what he had done. But he did expect, by God’s mercy, to know joy again.

He also knew what God wanted from him, and it was not self-punishment. “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17). Not a lifetime of misery. A heart that is broken and turns to him.

Where the past goes

Scripture uses vivid pictures for what God does with forgiven sin. “As far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12). “You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Micah 7:19). Hezekiah, spared from death, said to God, “you have cast all my sins behind your back” (Isaiah 38:17). God says through Isaiah, “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist” (Isaiah 44:22).

Most striking of all is the promise of the new covenant: “I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). God does not forget in the way we forget, as though the facts slipped his mind. He knows all things. But he chooses not to hold them against us, not to bring them up, not to treat us according to them. You may remember your sin every day. God, having forgiven it, does not keep it on the table between you.

Why this is not too good to be true

How can a holy God treat a forgiven past as if it no longer stood against us? Because it was dealt with at the cross. “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5). The regret you feel over your past is real, but Christ felt the full weight of God’s judgment on it. Every sin a believer regrets was already counted, already carried, already paid for on that day outside Jerusalem.

That is why the book of Hebrews can say that the blood of Christ will “purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:14). A conscience that keeps accusing you of sins already confessed is a conscience that has not yet fully heard the news. We may “draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience” (Hebrews 10:22).

Such were some of you

Paul wrote to a church full of people with pasts: thieves, drunkards, the sexually immoral, swindlers. Then he said, “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Notice the tense. “Such were.” Not “such are”. What you did is part of your history. In Christ it is no longer your identity.

This is the wonder of grace. God does not merely tolerate forgiven sinners. He clothes them in the righteousness of his Son and calls them his children. The regret that says, “This is who you really are,” is contradicted by the One whose verdict alone stands. “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

An example

A woman in her fifties ended a pregnancy at nineteen, frightened and alone. She came to faith ten years later and has told only her husband. In a quiet moment during the Lord’s Supper she hears the words, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). She has heard them a hundred times. This time she realises they include her, and that day too. She weeps, but differently.

For reflection

Read Psalm 51 slowly. Which line most fits your own heart? Which picture of forgiveness, the east and the west, the depths of the sea, God’s back, the blotted-out cloud, speaks most to you? What sins from your past do you keep on the table that God has already removed? What would change if you believed that “such were some of you” describes you?

4.title: The Rooster and the Charcoal Fire
4.essay:
Forgiveness clears the record. But Jesus does more than clear it. He comes back for people who have failed him and gives them a future. The stories of Peter and Paul show that a ruined past does not mean a wasted life.

Before the fall

On the night of his arrest, Jesus told Peter what was coming. “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:31–32). Read that slowly. Jesus knew Peter would deny him. He prayed for him before he fell. And he spoke of his restoration as certain: “when you have turned again”. Peter’s failure did not take Jesus by surprise, and it did not change his intentions toward him.

The same is true for you. Christ knew every failure of your life before you committed it. He went to the cross knowing it. If you belong to him, he is praying for you still.

And Peter

On the morning of the resurrection, the angel at the tomb gave the women a message: “go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee” (Mark 16:7). Two words, “and Peter”, carried a world of mercy. The one who had sworn he never knew Jesus was named. He had not been crossed off.

Another fire

In the courtyard Peter had stood by “a charcoal fire” (John 18:18), warming himself while he denied his Lord. Weeks later, by the Sea of Galilee, the risen Jesus made breakfast for his disciples, and when they came ashore “they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread” (John 21:9). John is the only Gospel writer to use that word, and only in these two places. Jesus brought Peter back, gently, to the scene of his worst memory.

Then he asked him three times, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). Three denials, three questions. “Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, ‘Do you love me?’” (John 21:17). It hurt. Restoration often does. But each answer was met not with a rebuke but with a task: “Feed my lambs.” “Tend my sheep.” “Feed my sheep.” And at the end, the same words with which it had all begun: “Follow me” (John 21:19).

Jesus did not pretend the denial had not happened. He walked Peter back through it. But he did so in order to give him a future, not to keep him in the past. The man who had failed in the courtyard became the shepherd of the flock, and on the day of Pentecost he preached to the very city where he had denied his Lord.

The chief of sinners

Paul’s past was darker still. Before his conversion he hunted Christians, imprisoned them and voted for their deaths. Years later he wrote, “though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13). He never minimised it. He called himself the foremost of sinners. And he said he was shown mercy for a reason: “that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16).

Paul’s past became a display case of Christ’s patience. Every person who thinks they are too far gone can look at Paul and see that they are not. “But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Forgetting what lies behind

So when Paul writes, “forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal” (Philippians 3:13–14), he is not telling us to pretend the past never happened. Paul clearly remembered his. In the context he is speaking of his old religious achievements, the things he once counted as gain. But the principle reaches further. To forget, in this sense, is to stop living there: neither leaning on past successes nor being crushed by past failures. A runner who keeps looking over his shoulder will stumble. The prize is ahead.

Notice why Paul can do this. He presses on “because Christ Jesus has made me his own” (Philippians 3:12). His hold on the future rested on Christ’s hold on him. The same is true for every believer. You can turn your face forward because you are held.

An example

A man who drank heavily through his twenties now leads a small group at church for men in recovery. When he first came to faith, he could not speak about those years without deep shame. He still does not glory in them. But when a young man sits across from him, shaking, and says, “You don’t know what I’ve done,” he is able to answer, “Actually, I might.” His worst years have become the very place where Christ uses him.

For reflection

What does it mean to you that Jesus prayed for Peter before he fell? Is there a “charcoal fire” in your life, a memory you avoid, that Christ may want to walk you back through in order to restore you? How is Paul’s past an encouragement to you? What would it look like for you to stop living in the past without pretending it never happened?

5.title: God Meant It for Good
5.essay:
“What if” imagines another life, the one that would have unfolded if we had chosen differently. But there is no other life. There is only this one, and it has always been in God’s hands, including the parts we most regret.

Joseph’s answer

When their father Jacob died, Joseph’s brothers were terrified. Surely now he would pay them back. They came and fell at his feet. Joseph wept, and said, “Do not fear, for am I in the place of God? As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today” (Genesis 50:19–20).

Notice what Joseph does not say. He does not say that what they did was good. He calls it evil. Nor does he say that God merely tidied up afterwards. He says God “meant it”. The same event had two intentions behind it: theirs, which was wicked, and God’s, which was gracious. Years earlier he had told them, “do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life” (Genesis 45:5).

Woven, not whitewashed

This is one of the deepest comforts in Scripture for anyone haunted by the past. God is sovereign over all things, even our sins and failures, yet he is never the author of sin. Our wrongs remain wrong. We remain responsible for them. But they have not escaped his rule, and they cannot defeat his purposes.

Christians have understood this in different ways. Many Arminian believers hold that God permits sin but does not ordain it, and then works to bring good out of it. Reformed believers hold that God ordains whatever comes to pass, including sinful acts, without himself doing evil, and that his plan includes the means, so our choices are real and our responsibility is real.

This commentary’s view: God governs all things, including the evil acts of people, so that he “meant it for good” in the very events where people meant harm, as the cross itself shows; yet he never does evil, and those who sin are truly accountable. This means that your failures, though truly yours and truly wrong, were never outside his hand. The study The Providence of God sets this out more fully.

So we must hold two things together. Never say, “It was fine, because God used it.” That would make light of the harm done. But never say, “I ruined God’s plan.” You did not. You are not that powerful.

All things for good

“And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). “All things” includes the worst things, our own sins among them. It does not mean that all things are good, or that we will always see the good in this life. The next verse tells us what the good is: to be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). God uses even our failures to make us more like Christ: humbler, gentler, more dependent, more grateful for grace.

Jacob, limping and blessed

Jacob’s life was a tangle of deceit, favouritism and grief. He wrestled with God at Peniel and came away blessed, but “limping because of his hip” (Genesis 32:31). He limped for the rest of his life. Yet at the end, blessing Joseph’s sons, he spoke of “the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil” (Genesis 48:15–16). The same man who had called his days “few and evil” now saw a shepherd’s hand through all of them. Hebrews remembers him not for his schemes but for his faith, “bowing in worship over the head of his staff” (Hebrews 11:21).

The years the locust ate

Many Christians have found comfort in God’s promise through Joel: “I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten” (Joel 2:25). It is a beautiful word, but it needs to be read carefully. In Joel, the locusts were a real judgment on a sinful people, and God promised that after they returned to him he would give back abundant harvests. He did not give back the lost years themselves. He gave plenty in place of famine.

So the promise is not that you will get your twenties back, or that the marriage will be as if it had never broken. It is that the God who disciplines also restores, and that his generosity can outrun our losses. Moses prayed something similar: “Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us, and for as many years as we have seen evil” (Psalm 90:15). Sometimes God answers that in this life. Fully, he will answer it in the next, when “he will wipe away every tear from their eyes” and say, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:4–5). Wasted years are not the end of the story. Eternity is long.

No other life

The “what if” mind imagines a better self in a better life. But that life never existed, and its happiness is imagined, not known. You do not know what the other road held. God does. “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15). The life you have, with its scars, is the one in which he has met you, and the one he is redeeming.

An example

A woman left a promising career to care for a sick parent, and later felt she had thrown her future away. Years on, her daughter is a nurse, and tells her that watching her mother care for grandma is why she chose the work. The career is still gone, and she still feels its loss at times. But she has begun to see a pattern in the weave that she could not see from the inside.

For reflection

How does Genesis 50:20 help you hold both the wrongness of your past and God’s rule over it? Do you ever feel that you ruined God’s plan for your life? How does Romans 8:28–29 answer that? What “locust years” do you grieve, and what would it mean to trust God with them, both now and in eternity?

6.title: Living with the Past
6.essay:
The past does not go away. Memories return. Some consequences remain. The question is not how to erase the past, but how to live with it before God, today and in the years ahead. Here is some practical wisdom, offered not as a way to earn peace, but as ways to live out the peace Christ has already won.

Tell the story truthfully to God

Many people carry their regrets in silence for years. David knew what that does: “For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3). Then: “I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity … and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5). Write it down if that helps. Tell God the whole story, plainly: what you did, what was done to you, what you did not know. Sort the strands: confess what was sin, admit what was folly, lament what was loss. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

Tell a trusted person

Some burdens grow lighter when they are spoken aloud to another believer: a pastor, an older friend, a counsellor. Hearing someone else say, “Christ has forgiven you,” can reach places that reading cannot. Choose someone wise and discreet.

Make amends where you can

When Zacchaeus met Jesus, his first instinct was to put things right: “if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). He did not do this to be forgiven. He did it because he had been. If there is an apology you can make, a debt you can repay or a lie you can correct, do it. An adult child may need to hear, “I was wrong in how I treated you, and I am sorry,” with no excuses attached.

But be wise. Some amends are no longer possible: the person has died, or cannot be found. Some would do more harm than good, such as reopening wounds for someone who has moved on, or making contact where it is unsafe. Where there has been abuse, never seek contact against the wishes of the one harmed. Take counsel before acting. “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18). Where nothing more can be done, leave it with God.

Grieve the consequences that remain

Forgiveness is full, but it does not always remove the earthly results of what we did. David was forgiven, yet his child died. A divorce may be forgiven and the family still divided. Years of neglect may be forgiven and a son still distant. It is right to grieve this. Notice what David did when the child died: he “arose from the earth and washed … And he went into the house of the LORD and worshiped” (2 Samuel 12:20). He grieved, then got up and worshipped. Lament is not the opposite of faith. Psalm after psalm shows God’s people pouring out sorrow to him.

Refuse the replay

When the old scene begins to play again, you do not have to sit and watch it. Recognise it: “Here is that memory again.” If there is a new thing to confess or do, deal with it. If not, turn deliberately away. Speak back to it: “That sin was nailed to the cross. I will not pay for it again.” Then turn your mind to God, as the writer of Lamentations did when his soul was bowed down by memory: “But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:21–23). This is what it means to “take every thought captive to obey Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). It takes practice, and the replay will return. Each time you turn, the path grows easier.

Let your past comfort others

God “comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God” (2 Corinthians 1:4). Jesus told Peter, “when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). In time, and with wisdom about what to share, your regrets may become someone else’s hope.

After an abortion

Women and men who have been involved in an abortion often carry a silent grief for decades: around due dates, at the sight of a child of the age theirs would have been, or when the subject comes up at church. If that is you, please hear this tenderly. Your child was a real person, and it is right to grieve. Your sin is real too, and it is forgiven in full for all who trust in Christ. Many have found it helpful to name the child before God, and to entrust that little one to his mercy, with real hope. Many churches and pregnancy centres offer post-abortion support groups. You do not have to carry this alone. The study Life & Death Ethics says more.

When regret becomes depression

For some, regret sinks into something heavier: weeks of low mood, sleeplessness, loss of appetite, inability to enjoy anything, or constant self-accusation that no truth seems to reach. This may be depression, which is common and treatable. Please see your doctor. Counselling and, where prescribed, medicine are good gifts of God, and using them is no failure of faith. The study Depression & the Christian says more.

If you are thinking of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust.

An example

The retired man from the first chapter finally tells his pastor about his son. Together they pray, and he writes a short letter, owning his failures without asking for anything back. His son does not reply for months. When he does, it is a single line: “Thanks, Dad. Maybe we could get a coffee.” Some evenings the old memories still come on his walk. Now, when they do, he prays for his son instead.

For reflection

Is there a story you need to tell truthfully to God, or to a trusted person? Is there an amend you can still make, or one you need to leave with God? What will you do the next time the replay begins? How might God use your past to comfort someone else?
